title: LifeLine.ai: A SigLIP-MedGemma Multimodal Framework with KTO Alignment for Open-Vocabulary 12-Lead ECG Report Generation
abstract: Automated twelve-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) interpretation has historically relied on discriminative classifiers limited to closed-set diagnostic labels, signal reconstruction, or saliency heatmaps. While categorizing predefined arrhythmias well, these static classifiers cannot generate narrative clinical reports, incorporate patient history, or support interactive clinical question-answering (Q&A). We present LifeLine.ai, an end-toend multimodal Vision-ECG-Language framework for automated cardiac diagnosis and clinical reporting. After early attempts at waveform peak-tracking and coordinate mapping failed against complex morphological variations, we leveraged large-scale PhysioNet repositories (MIMIC-IV and PTB-XL). Because hardware limits precluded training on over 800,000 raw records, we curated a balanced subset to estimate performance, converting one-dimensional signals into 3x4 twelve-lead grids with continuous Lead II rhythm strips at the bottom. Our pipeline integrates YOLOv11s localization, a LoRAadapted Google SigLIP encoder, a trainable Multi-Layer Perceptron projector, and a 4-bit quantized MedGemma-4B model, complemented by a separate Kahneman-Tversky Optimization (KTO) pipeline built on collected user feedback and a multi-LLM consensus engine. On this compact subset, SigLIP outperformed Swin Transformer encodings (~0.21 vs. ~0.25 validation loss), achieving 71.0% open-vocabulary precision and a 75.0% contextual F1 score across a cloud deployment spanning Vercel, mobile apps, Amazon EC2, Firebase, Hugging Face, Modal GPUs, and lifelinecg-sdk. Our code is available at https://github.com/Asad939asad/ LifeLine.ai-.

title: Scalable frameworks for local evaluation of AI-enabled imaging devices using PACS-integrated large language models
abstract: Introduction: Artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled imaging device performance may vary across institutions due to differences in disease prevalence, patient demographics, and acquisition protocols. Routine local evaluation, including pre-deployment baseline testing and post-deployment monitoring, remains limited by manual data curation. A large language model (LLM)-as-a-judge approach using existing radiology reports provides a method of performing local evaluation. Methods: We established PACS-integrated LLMs in HIPAA-compliant environments. We then developed two scalable frameworks to automate key processes of local evaluation: selection of a candidate series for device inference and generation of report-derived labels. We applied these frameworks to 4,000 consecutive non-contrast head CT examinations from two hospitals to evaluate agreement between radiology reports and Purple AI Hyper Insight-ICH, a commercial intracranial hemorrhage detection device. Results: For series selection, we used a three-tiered, traffic-light approach across 31,422 available series to select a single series for device inference in 3,976 examinations. For radiology report field extraction, we refined an LLM prompt with three steps: initial binary classification, characterization of discordance between the binary classification prompt output and device output, and a comprehensive prompt (featuring 28 structured fields that were informed by the preceding stages). The positive percent agreement (PPA) depended on the definition of positive cases based on the comprehensive prompt fields: it was 87.7% (79.2 to 95.0%) using similar criteria to many published studies (acute or acute-on-chronic, non-minimal, non-equivocal hemorrhage), yet was lower when including chronic, minimal or equivocal ICH. The negative percent agreement (NPA) was 94.7% (94.0 to 95.4%). Subgroup analyses demonstrated that discrepancies involving a positive device output commonly occurred in the setting of recent intracranial surgery and intracranial hyperdense (non-hemorrhagic) lesions. Conclusion: A PACS-integrated LLM approach, together with scalable frameworks for series selection and label generation, can provide radiologists with local insights about AI-enabled device performance. These insights may help radiologists interpret device outputs in clinical practice, particularly in scenarios associated with greater device-report discordance.

title: EATS: Scaling Tool-Use Experience for Medical Reasoning Agents
abstract: Medical reasoning agents combine large language model (LLM) reasoning with clinical workflows and specialized neural tools. However, general-purpose LLMs receive limited training exposure to domain-specific medical tools, and the uncertainty and distributional shifts of neural tool outputs make selecting tools from simple descriptions significantly more challenging than in deterministic settings such as calculators or dictionary lookups. In this paper, we propose EATS, an experience-augmented tool selection strategy that leverages accumulated tool-use trajectories to improve tool selection in medical reasoning agents. EATS constructs a memory of past interactions, including queries, tool choices, arguments, and self-evaluated feedback, and retrieves relevant experiences to guide tool selection for new queries. As memory construction does not require ground-truth supervision, EATS scales naturally with test-time experience. We evaluate EATS on tool-augmented medical reasoning tasks, including closed-ended visual question answering and free-form report generation. Experiments on four public datasets, ChestAgentBench, CheXbench, MIMIC-CXR, and SLAKE-VQA, across three multimodal LLMs, Qwen3-VL 2B, Qwen3-VL 32B, and GPT-5.5, show consistent gains in tool selection behavior and downstream medical reasoning performance. Code is available at https://github.com/Limingyuan001/EATS.

title: Large Language Model Agents for Evidence Based Genetic Disease Severity Classification
abstract: Disease severity classification for genetic conditions is subjective and labor-intensive, creating bottlenecks in genomic screening, where commercial panels vary widely in size and overlap. We developed an autonomous AI agent integrating Reasoning and Acting (ReAct) with Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) to classify 10,211 Human Phenotype Ontology terms. It uses American College of Medical Genetics (ACMG)-endorsed severity guidelines and American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) quality-of-life criteria to retrieve PubMed literature, generate interpretable reasoning chains, and independently verify claims. At the phenotype level, using expert-curated cohorts, the agent achieved 93.55% accuracy (MCC 0.9237) with 82.6% to 91.4% of claims supported by direct evidence or valid inferences. Gene-level severity was aggregated across 8,738 pairs, identifying 3,283 autosomal recessive pairs with severe or profound presentations. External validation showed 95.2% concordance with Mackenzie's Mission gene list. This system enables standardized panel design by providing reliable, automated classification supported by direct evidence.

title: The unedited acceptance rate: a review-fidelity metric for human-in-the-loop clinical AI
abstract: Objective. Guidance for large language model (LLM) drafting in clinical care relies on human review, yet review is rarely measured as a control. We aimed to define computable measures of review fidelity, establish which a deployed system can compute, and pre-specify their first analysis. Materials and Methods. For a multi-agent clinical system in routine use at one private London outpatient clinic, we defined acceptance coverage, attribution completeness, the unedited acceptance rate (UAR), a bounded normalized edit distance, availability latency and an unedited fast-approval rate (UFA). We checked each measure against the system's code and database structure at a fixed commit on four approval routes and pre-specified a prospective 12-week analysis. Results. The UAR equals the mass at zero of the edit-distance distribution, and availability latency bounds reading time from above only. Clinical documentation keeps draft and signed text with a recorded signer, so the core measures are computable there. Help-desk edit telemetry is written only when the agent's version has been stored. The WhatsApp agent route records no edit signal, and its approver need not be named. No route records when a draft is opened. Documentation accept events were not written before a change committed on November 16, 2026. Model-generated content, including live voice-agent speech, also reaches patients without approval. No measured values are reported. Discussion. Acceptance alone cannot separate accurate drafts from approval without reading, and three of four routes cannot yet support the family. Conclusion. Review fidelity can be specified as telemetry at the approval event. Validation against missed errors is required.

title: Beyond the Chatbot: Agentic Artificial Intelligence and the Future of Infectious Disease Practice.
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) discourse in infectious disease (ID) has focused on benchmarking large language model chatbots against clinicians, a useful but narrowing inquiry. Agentic AI is a different paradigm: goal-directed systems that pursue clinical objectives over time, integrating data, invoking tools, monitoring results, and adapting without repeated prompting. This Viewpoint defines the anatomy of an agent, situates it within a 3-level framework (predictive, conversational, agentic), and examines how agents could transform 6 domains of ID practice: clinical care, antimicrobial stewardship, clinical microbiology, infection prevention and control, research, and epidemiology and pandemic preparedness. Individual components have proven value; integrated systems remain untested. No validated agentic system has been deployed in clinical ID; error propagation, algorithmic bias, cost, absent validation frameworks, undefined liability, and consequences for the workforce and its training must be addressed first. The ID community has a narrow window to shape these systems before decisions are made without it.

title: Beyond Hard Tokens: Predictive Memory for Multimodal Protein Generation
abstract: Multimodal protein language models unify sequence and discrete structural tokens via iterative masked decoding, offering a promising paradigm for joint protein design. However, standard decoders rely on a memoryless mask reset at each iteration: only a sparse subset of newly committed hard tokens is carried forward, while all remaining unresolved sites are reset to an identical [MASK] embedding. In open-ended co-generation where neither modality provides a fixed external anchor, this stateless transition limits single-step refinement depth and deprives both tracks of stable cross-step soft anchors, leading to slow convergence or degenerative repetitive collapse. Observing that uncommitted predictions evolve with pronounced temporal coherence rather than erratic noise, we introduce Predictive Memory (PredMem), a training-free self-conditioning recurrence that carries these soft beliefs across steps. At each step, PredMem summarizes raw logits into a probability-weighted Top-$k$ expectation embedding at every residue and affinely interpolates it into eligible masked inputs on the next step at zero extra denoiser cost. Across DPLM-2, DPLM-2.1, and ESM3, PredMem raises unconditional sequence-structure co-generation success by 3.6, 17.7, and 48.7 percentage points, respectively, while improving the quality-diversity trade-off and suppressing repetitive mode collapse. Controlled diagnostics show that these gains stem primarily from early trajectory stabilization in unanchored cross-modal co-evolution rather than extra compute or simple entropy reduction, establishing PredMem as an efficient inference mechanism for multimodal discrete generation.

title: Unjamming Deferrals: Supporting Students Through JAMN Bot, a Mobile RAG-Grounded Policy Assistant
abstract: In some educational institutions, workflows such as the exam deferral process can be slow, inconvenient, and inconsistent, which creates the need to implement novel digital systems. This paper presents Schedulater, a mobile app for managing university exam deferrals. JAMN Bot is a Large Language Model (LLM)-powered chatbot integrated into Schedulater that provides context-aware support to help users understand the deferral process. The system features a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipeline using Ollama (Llama 3.2 3B) for self-hosted inference which enables policy-grounded responses without sacrificing privacy. We evaluate the system using a 43-item benchmark spanning Exam Deferral, Privacy, Scheduling, Cross-Policy, and Adversarial & Out-of-Scope questions, and report inter-rater agreement among our human evaluators alongside retrieval hit-rate metrics. Subsequently, we utilize an LLM-as-a-judge approach with GPT-5.4, revealing slight-to-moderate alignment with our raters that improves with answer quality, and check the ranking against a panel including Gemini 3.5 Flash and Qwen3.5 397B. The results of our study display trade-offs between open-weight and frontier models, as well as LLM-human evaluation alignment with answer quality. Schedulater demonstrates the feasibility of integrating lightweight LLMs into university administrative workflows with structured retrieval.

title: BLADE: Better Language Answers through Dialogue and Explanations
abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based educational assistants often provide direct answers offering little incentive for students to explore or engage with course materials. We present BLADE (Better Language Answers through Dialogue and Explanations), a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) based conversational assistant grounded in course-specific content that guides students toward relevant materials through citation-grounded dialogue rather than delivering unsourced solutions. We evaluate BLADE in an advanced undergraduate NLP course with extensive instructional resources, in which locating and synthesizing relevant material is a central challenge. During quizzes, students are assigned to one of three conditions: BLADE only, direct course materials only, or both; we measure performance and resource usage. Results show that students consistently select BLADE over direct materials when both are available, and that quiz performance is highest when students use BLADE alone. In contrast, simultaneous use of both resources is associated with significantly lower performance. No statistically significant difference in quiz performance occurred between assigned resource conditions. These findings show the potential of RAG-based assistants as a citation-grounded interface for applying course content under open-book exam-like conditions, while suggesting that adding direct-material access does not necessarily improve in-task performance.

title: Toward systems-level analysis of medical incident reports: A clinician-annotated evaluation of large language models using HFACS
abstract: Objectives: We aimed to assess agreement between reviewers in factor extraction and Human Factors Analysis and Classification System (HFACS) classification, and between large language model (LLM) classifications and reviewer-consensus reference standards, using public medical incident reports from Japan. Methods: Six clinicians in three pairs reviewed 150 records with artificial intelligence (AI)-generated fault tree analysis (FTA) candidates and 60 new records without AI candidates, creating pair-consensus reference standards (RSv1 and RSv2). We assessed classification agreement, factor-extraction micro-F1, and FTA versus direct classification. Reviewers reassessed RSv2 after additional public information. AI classification was also evaluated on fixed RSv2 factors. Results: Pooled inter-reviewer detailed-category kappa in RSv1 was 0.503 (95% CI, 0.456 to 0.548). In the final RSv1 evaluation (37 records; 306 leaves), kappa was 0.427 (0.359 to 0.493) for GPT-5.6 Sol and 0.499 (0.445 to 0.551) for secondary Kimi K2.6. Neither estimate reached the detailed-category kappa target of 0.6. FTA-based structural rankings and factor-frequency rankings selected identical top-five categories; the FTA-minus-direct-classification micro-F1 difference was 0.032 (-0.024 to 0.086). RSv2 factor-extraction micro-F1 was 0.420 (0.303 to 0.527), using AI-assisted semantic matching; 23/60 RSv2 records were analysable with uncertainty and 22/60 were not analysable. Responses without uncertainty accounted for 37.5% before and 46.7% after reassessment; pooled linear weighted kappa for inter-reviewer analysability agreement was 0.386 and 0.203. Exploratory AI classification of 75 RSv2 factors with a single HFACS label yielded detailed-category kappa 0.240 (0.101 to 0.390). Conclusions: Disagreement persisted in the extraction and classification of contributing factors from public medical incident reports, including in reviewer assessments, and the tested FTA approach did not establish added value. Difficulty obtaining sufficiently specific contextual information from the available narratives may have contributed to these judgement difficulties, consistent with concerns raised in previous studies. Organisations that operate incident reporting systems or develop reporting guidance could strengthen reporting processes so that the specific circumstances and context needed to interpret contributing factors and relationships are recorded.

title: PerovAgent: Autonomous Ligand Design for Halide Perovskite Nanocrystals
abstract: Designing surface-capping ligands for high-performance halide perovskite nanocrystals requires navigating a vast molecular space while discovering design rules that govern ligand-surface interactions. Here, we introduce PerovAgent, an autonomous multi-agent framework that combines large language model (LLM)-driven scientific reasoning with computational tools for atomistic model construction, machine-learned interatomic potential evaluation, and statistical validation. Across ten independent campaigns on CsPbBr3 surfaces, PerovAgent adaptively explored and refined diverse ligand chemistries while progressively improving the binding-energy objective. Beyond optimization, the framework converts recurring chemical observations into explicit design principles that can be statistically evaluated. Of 35 formulated principles, 19 were prospectively supported, of which seven also passed the confound audit, highlighting the need to systematically validate plausible LLM-generated hypotheses during autonomous discovery. A recurrent alkynyl-phosphonate principle was further examined using density functional theory, which reproduced the predicted energetic preference. These results demonstrate an autonomous discovery framework that not only searches molecular space and optimizes the scalar objective but also transforms its search trajectory into systematically testable design principles. The framework can also be extended to more complex ligands, including zwitterionic, multidentate, and polymerizable ligands, to explore a wider range of ligand-surface interactions and uncover new design principles for halide perovskite nanocrystals.

title: Joint Representation of Valence and Arousal in the Human Brain
abstract: Scenes varying in emotional content are commonly characterized along two affective dimensions: hedonic valence, reflecting pleasantness, and emotional arousal, reflecting intensity. Although prior studies have examined neural representations of valence and arousal separately, it remains unclear how these dimensions are represented jointly and how their representation relates to low-level visual and scene-level properties. Here, we used representational similarity analysis (RSA) to identify brain regions whose activity patterns represented the joint valence-arousal structure of affective images and to compare this representation with those of low-level visual and scene-level properties. Twenty participants viewed 60 International Affective Picture System (IAPS) images during simultaneous EEG-fMRI recording. We constructed three image-level representational dissimilarity matrices (RDMs): an Emotion RDM derived from valence and arousal ratings; a GIST RDM derived from low-level visual features captured by GIST descriptors; and a Scene RDM derived from CLIP-ViT image embeddings. Searchlight fMRI RSA identified joint valence-arousal representations in lateral occipitotemporal cortex, low-level visual representations in visual cortex, with smaller extensions into right STS and right insula, and scene-level representations across distributed occipital, temporal, parietal, and frontal regions. The valence-arousal representation showed little spatial overlap with the low-level visual representation but was spatially nested within regions representing scene-level properties. EEG-fMRI fusion further indicated that low-level visual representations emerged at approximately 124 ms after stimulus onset, followed by scene-level and valence-arousal representations at approximately 428 ms and 532 ms, respectively. Together, these findings suggest that joint valence-arousal representations are linked to higher-order scene representations, are distinct from low-level visual representations in both space and time, and may support the affective-semantic characterization of visual scenes. Exploratory analyses further showed that valence and arousal ratings generated by multimodal large language models (ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini) corresponded closely with human ratings and yielded neural representation maps that substantially overlapped with the human valence-arousal map.

title: Unscored variants leave many comparisons of variant effect predictors undecided: evidence from ClinVar, published benchmarks and genomic language models
abstract: Background. Variant effect predictors leave different variants unscored, so reported accuracies often rest on different variants, and which predictor is better can depend on variants never scored. Results. Manski's sharp bounds contain each predictor's accuracy and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) whatever its unscored variants would score. A comparison is decided when the two bounds are disjoint, which cannot happen when the two shares scored (of variants or, for AUROC, pathogenic-benign pairs) sum to one or less. For 49 dbNSFP predictors on 328,328 ClinVar substitutions, 745 of 1,176 comparisons are undecided inside declared scopes and 1,093 on the whole panel. In ten benchmarks from one PubMed query, 1,045 of 2,842 stated orderings (36.8%) are undecided. Yet most orderings between well-known predictors are decided (177 of 287), among them AlphaMissense above REVEL in the sixth Critical Assessment of Genome Interpretation. AlphaMissense's canonical-transcript release scores no missense substitution in secondary-findings genes CALM1, CALM2 or WT1, and missense variants that REVEL's and AlphaMissense's releases leave unscored are pathogenic less often than the panel's (likelihood ratios 0.18 and 0.25, describing each release). Across nine species, the genomic language model Evo 2 does not outperform gene annotation (species-mean AUROC 0.943 against 0.958); its 8,192-bp margin is resolved over Ensembl's conservation track (+0.108) but not over the 241-mammal phyloP (+0.055). Conclusions. Benchmarks should report each predictor's reach (share of variants scored) per label class and which orderings the bounds decide; the deposited reach matrices and glmtrust package allow these checks without rescoring.

title: Alignment-Aware Genomic Coordinate Encoding for Long-Range DNA Modeling
abstract: Current genomic foundation models (GFMs) largely inherit the language-modeling paradigm over contiguous token sequences, treating DNA as ordinary text. The genome, however, is a coordinate-based system of sparse signals: variants, regulatory elements, and distal gene interactions occupy a vanishing fraction of chromosome-scale sequences and are defined by their positions in the reference coordinate system rather than by linear proximity. This mismatch limits pure sequence modeling on individualized, non-contiguous genomic tasks. We present USM-AA, a genomic foundation model built on two complementary components: an alignment embedding module (AEM) that explicitly represents each token's chromosome, strand, and comparison outcome against the reference, making variant signals directly observable; and an Alignment-Aware Rotary Position Embedding (AARoPE) that places tokens on the reference coordinate system, preserving correct positional relationships over non-contiguous inputs while supporting end-to-end training. USM-AA is further trained with a reverse-complement masked learning strategy that operates purely at the loss level, adding no parameters or architectural modification. Pretrained on large-scale genomic sequences spanning cross-species evolution and human population variation, USM-AA achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple genomic tasks, including long-range regulatory prediction and variant-effect prediction. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/Jimmy0743/USM-AA.

title: Distinguishing Social Isolation, Social Support, and Contextual False Positives in Clinical Notes Using Fine-Tuned Language Models: Multisite Validation Study
abstract: Background: Social isolation and social support are clinically important but inconsistently represented in structured electronic health record data. Their identification from clinical narratives is complicated by nuanced, context-dependent language and by variation in how social connectedness is documented across clinical settings, patient populations, and geographic locations. Models intended for health care use must therefore distinguish social isolation from documented support, negation, ambiguous social circumstances, and non-social clinical uses of similar terminology while remaining robust to differences in documentation practices. Objective: This study aimed to develop and evaluate locally deployable, fine-tuned language models for context-aware classification of social isolation, social support, and contextually similar non-relevant clinical text across multiple health systems. Materials and Methods: We conducted a retrospective study using electronic health record data from 326,847 adults aged 50 years or older who received care at 3 Tennessee health systems from 2020 to 2023. Candidate clinical text was identified using social-environment ICD-10-CM Z codes and an established social isolation lexicon. Human annotators classified 9,748 spans from 9,578 clinical notes contributed by 6,881 patients as social isolation, social support, or no social isolation. The annotated corpus included social isolation and support concepts including negations, infection-control and microbiology terminology, institutional living arrangements, and other contextually ambiguous examples. FLAN-T5-Large, BERT, RoBERTa, and Gemma-2-2B were fine-tuned for 3-class span classification. Full fine-tuning and parameter-efficient fine-tuning using low-rank adaptation approaches were evaluated for the best performing model, FLAN-T5-Large. Performance was assessed using site-based internal-external cross-validation, with macro-F1 as the primary metric. Results: The annotated corpus included 2,318 social isolation spans, 638 social support spans, and 6,792 spans classified as no social isolation. Fully fine-tuned FLAN-T5-Large achieved the best performance, with a mean macro-F1 of 0.90 (SD 0.01). Class-specific F1 scores were 0.85 (SD 0.03) for social isolation, 0.87 (SD 0.04) for social support, and 0.96 (SD 0.02) for no social isolation. Gemma-2-2B achieved a macro-F1 of 0.85 (SD 0.01), compared with 0.84 (SD 0.06) for RoBERTa and 0.86 (SD 0.06) for BERT. Full fine-tuning also outperformed parameter-efficient fine-tuning in secondary pooled analyses (macro-F1 0.93 vs 0.90) in the corresponding held-out evaluation for the FLAN-T5-Large model. Remaining errors primarily involved patients who lived alone but received assistance, family presence without meaningful support, grief-related language, and non-social clinical uses of isolation terminology. Conclusions: Fine-tuned language models can distinguish social isolation, social support, and contextually similar but unrelated language across heterogeneous clinical settings. FLAN-T5-Large provided the strongest and most stable performance, including for the less frequent social support class. The 3-class annotation framework, inclusion of difficult negative examples, and multisite evaluation offer a practical approach for converting nuanced social-connectedness documentation into structured data. Further work should evaluate end-to-end identification in unselected clinical notes and prospective integration into clinical and population health workflows.

title: RSI-PDEbench: A Benchmark for Self-Improving Agents in PDE Solving
abstract: Identifying and solving partial differential equations (PDEs) from sampled solution data often requires substantial expert effort in equation discovery, coefficient estimation, and numerical solver configuration, especially under noise and distribution shifts. Can large language model (LLM) agents automate this workflow accurately and efficiently? To investigate this question, we introduce RSI-PDEbench, a benchmark of 1,001 cases spanning 42 equation templates, including both classical and fractional PDEs. It provides three evaluation settings: Full evaluates performance on noise-free solution data; Noisy tests robustness to Gaussian noise with an RMS equal to 50\% of the clean-signal RMS; and Hard-OOD tests challenging out-of-distribution generalization to unseen equation templates and shifted coefficient ranges. We further introduce RSI-PDE, a recursively self-improving agent harness that shortlists candidate equations by residual loss, uses relative $L^2$ feedback to refine coefficients and numerical solvers, and applies a validation gate to policy and memory updates. We compare RSI-PDE with single-run baselines and native agent harnesses (Claude Code or Codex) across four frontier models. Across the three settings, RSI-PDE improves the pass rate averaged across the four models by 106.5--181.9\% relative to single-run baselines and by 3.0--19.6\% relative to native harnesses, while reducing total recorded model calls by 46.9\% across the 12 model--setting pairs. These results highlight the potential of validated recursive self-improvement in LLM agents to advance scientific computing.

title: Towards Explainable Industrial Anomaly Detection via Knowledge-Guided Latent Reasoning
abstract: Industrial anomaly detection demands precise reasoning over fine-grained defect patterns. However, existing multimodal large language models (MLLMs), pretrained on general-domain data, often struggle to capture category-specific anomalies, thereby limiting both detection accuracy and interpretability. To address these limitations, we propose Reason-IAD, a knowledge-guided dynamic latent reasoning framework for explainable industrial anomaly detection. Reason-IAD comprises two core components. First, a retrieval-augmented knowledge module incorporates category-specific textual descriptions into the model input, enabling context-aware reasoning over domain-specific defects. Second, an entropy-driven latent reasoning mechanism conducts iterative exploration within a compact latent space using optimizable latent think tokens, guided by an entropy-based reward that encourages confident and stable predictions. Furthermore, a dynamic visual injection strategy selectively incorporates the most informative image patches into the latent sequence, directing the reasoning process toward regions critical for anomaly detection. Extensive experimental results demonstrate that Reason-IAD consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods across multiple tasks. The code will be publicly available at https://github.com/chenpeng052/Reason-IAD.

title: Deciphering Molecular Language for Spectral Interpretation with a Foundation Model Pretrained on Repository-Wide Metabolomics Data
abstract: In-depth, scalable structural interpretation of tandem mass spectra from diverse biological tissues and environmental samples is essential for understanding the molecular diversity of cellular environments and the metabolic architecture of living systems. Although community-driven resources such as GNPS and MassIVE have aggregated massive volumes of tandem mass spectra spanning a wide range of organisms, clinical cohorts and environmental surveys, modeling and interpreting this exponentially expanding spectral corpus to distill molecular information and derive meaningful biological insights poses a fundamental challenge for established computational methods. Here we present UltraMS, a dual-polarity foundation model tailored to decipher the molecular language latent in tandem mass spectra through large-scale pretraining on more than 160 million spectra encompassing both positive and negative ion modes. Our findings illustrate that UltraMS is capable of effectively decoding the chemical semantics of molecules underlying mass spectra via self-supervised learning, achieving superior performance across a variety of downstream tasks, including elemental detection, molecular identification, molecular property profiling, and metabolic landscape characterization. Remarkably, UltraMS enables conducting molecular identification with fine-grained spectral interpretability, simultaneously elucidating molecular structures from untargeted MS/MS spectra and providing peak-by-peak substructural attributions via annotation transfer. Deployed on a clinical cohort of human plaque samples, UltraMS demonstrates significant potential in discovering previously unrecognized phenotype-linked metabolites supported by structurally grounded fragment-ion formation pathways, while effectively correcting likely misannotated clinical markers. Furthermore, building on the structure-aware spectral representations learned by UltraMS, we construct UltraAtlas, a chemical-property-resolved map that organizes millions of experimental spectra into a unified coordinate system, enabling millisecond-scale molecular profiling and offering practical guidance for exploratory navigation across vast chemical space. Applied to human scalp metabolomics, UltraAtlas effectively captures distinct metabolic variations across individuals, highlighting phenotype-specific chemical signatures while shedding light on the chemical niches of the resident microbiome. Together, UltraMS and UltraAtlas constitute a generalizable framework for structural elucidation and biological discovery from tandem mass spectra, empowering the comprehensive exploration of the largely undeciphered metabolomes across different domains of life.

title: CLOVER: Chemical-gene LLM benchmark for obtaining valid entity relationships for the Comparative Toxicogenomics Database (CTD)
abstract: Objective: The Comparative Toxicogenomics Database (CTD) provides expert-curated chemical-gene interactions about environmental exposure effects on human diseases. Existing automated relation extraction systems are typically restricted to 3-10 interaction types and operate on abstracts only. We introduce CLOVER, a systematic benchmark for evaluating large language models (LLMs) on full-text chemical-gene interaction extraction using CTD-defined chemical-gene interaction terminology. The framework is designed to support 47 base interactions with directional modifiers (increase, decrease, affects), yielding 136 possible supported interaction classes. Evaluation is restricted to the subset of classes represented in the selected articles. Methods: CLOVER processes 50 full-text PubMed Central articles (1,563 sections) with PubTator and CTD integration. The pipeline consists of four stages: (1) LLM Extraction with one-shot and few-shot prompting; (2) LLM Validation to confirm and revise interactions; (3) Rule-based Refinement of extracted interactions to standardize terminology and eliminate errors; and (4) Human Review for expert oversight. We benchmark four LLMs (GPT-4.1, GPT-4o, Claude-Sonnet-4.5, and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash) and compare against a naive baseline that applies unstructured prompting directly to full-text PDFs. Results: The naive baseline achieves only 13% recall and 36% precision. Refinement significantly enhances performance by eliminating unsupported interactions. Under strict limitations, Claude-Sonnet-4.5 alone achieves 72% recall and 61% precision, and Claude with self-validation achieves 74% recall and 49% precision compared to CTD. Of the 136 supported interaction classes, 17 were represented in our evaluation. Conclusion: To our knowledge, CLOVER establishes the first benchmark for full-text chemical-gene interaction extraction aligned with CTD. Our findings demonstrate that CLOVER achieves workable metrics for CTD-aligned curation relative to minimal whole-PDF prompting. This study addresses only a fraction of the content manually curated in CTD; considerably more work is needed to advance LLM-based tools to determine the extent to which these tools can approximate the full capacity of manual curation at CTD.

title: Validating LLM judges for automated oversight of patient communication
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to mediate patient communication, yet scalable evaluation of their safety, accuracy, and communication quality remains an open problem. LLM judges have emerged as automated evaluators, but whether they can holistically replicate human expert judgment is unvalidated. Informed consent for clinical trials presents a demanding case because it requires conveying complex information to lay audiences under ethical and safety constraints. We developed a seven-criterion evaluation rubric informed by multiple stakeholder groups, spanning safety and ethics, reliability, and communication quality. We validated the rubric on the Informed CONsent Benchmark (ICON-Bench) and evaluated 19 LLM judges across multiple implementation strategies on 800 oncology and 200 non-oncology question-answer pairs. Clinician reference ratings showed strong interrater reliability. LLM judges showed high sensitivity for safety violations and stronger correlations with clinician ratings for factual accuracy than for communication quality. Safety-specialized guard models underperformed general-purpose and medical-purpose LLM judges. Patient advocates gave lower mean usefulness scores than clinicians and LLM judges, but rated clarity and succinctness similarly to clinicians and higher than LLM judges. These findings support LLM judges as a complement to human review of informed consent communication. Further work could improve LLM judge alignment with patient perspectives.

title: Familiar Words, Unfamiliar Minds: Conventionalization without Calibration in the Vocabulary of Mind
abstract: Speakers describe new technologies by stretching old words, letting experience of the new referents sort out which inferences carry over. I argue that stretching the vocabulary of mind to language models pulls apart two processes that theories of metaphor and linguistic change tend to conflate: conventionalization, whereby a stretched word ceases to be marked as such, and calibration, whereby the inferences it invites are fitted to what its new referents bear out. As a gene variant can reach fixation without being an adaptation, a word can become conventional without being calibrated. A corpus study of "hallucinate" in 8,568 abstracts and 31,866 forum comments shows conventionalization running most of its course within three years. Calibration need not keep pace: these models are organized so unlike human minds that it is hard to tell when mental words apply and what they imply. Even warranted attributions can mislead: mechanistic analysis shows that a transformer trained to navigate Manhattan has and uses a faithful street map, yet loses track of its position on long, diverted journeys. Nor is the gap likely to close by itself. The usual routes to calibration (direct experience, designers' knowledge, experiment) presuppose a referent that is accessible, stable, and independent of the discourse about it. But language models are opaque, fast-changing, and looped into the discourse: they are trained on past uses of mental vocabulary and on the experimental literature about them, and join the discourse themselves. Calibration must therefore be organized, through a reciprocal, not merely deferential, division of linguistic labour. This yields a norm of targeted qualification (flag the specific inferences an attribution invites without support), a reply to the worry that meaning change eludes deliberate control, and three testable predictions about when qualifications calibrate expectations.

title: Validating Multi-Model AI-Generated Acceptance Criteria in Requirements Engineering
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in software engineering to generate artifacts such as requirements, user stories, acceptance criteria, documentation, and code. Their use in requirements engineering raises important questions about correctness, traceability, and hallucination, especially because flawed specifications can affect later design, implementation, and verification activities. While much recent work on AI-assisted software engineering has focused on code generation and code-level validation, the validation of AI-generated specifications has received less attention. This paper addresses this gap by presenting a validation-oriented approach for AI-generated acceptance criteria. The approach combines retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), multi-model generation, and an explicitly structured human-in-the-loop workflow. We describe a working prototype that allows users to prepare or enter user stories, generate acceptance criteria using several LLMs, optionally augment generation with retrieved requirements-related examples, compare outputs side by side, inspect retrieved context, and select, edit, or regenerate candidate criteria before explicitly submitting a reviewer-finalized version. The system also records model outputs, user interventions, retrieval settings, and final criteria as part of a logged decision process. Rather than claiming that generation accuracy is already improved, the contribution of this work is to operationalize validation as an explicit, inspectable, and accountable process for AI-generated requirements artifacts.

title: Efficient Video Retrieval Augmented Generation via Token Allocation
abstract: Efficient long-video understanding requires identifying relevant evidence while minimizing the tokens processed by vision-language models (VLMs). Existing video retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) methods rely on frame selection and token compression, but overlook how much each additional token is worth. We introduce Lembas, a plug-and-play framework that formulates video RAG as a token allocation problem over frames and subtitles under a shared budget. Our key insight is that the value of a token diminishes within each item and decreases further as similar evidence receives more tokens. Lembas captures both effects in a single objective and solves it with an efficient iterative water-filling algorithm that has a provable convergence guarantee. For multi-turn conversations, Lembas reuses the tokens processed in earlier turns and refines relevance with the VLM's attention at no extra cost. Our evaluations show that Lembas improves accuracy by up to 7.2 percentage points over state-of-the-art baselines at comparable compute. On multi-turn video understanding, Lembas achieves up to 1.5 percentage points higher accuracy with 1.7-17.3x fewer TFLOPs.

title: ML-Tool-Bench: Tool-Augmented Planning for ML Tasks
abstract: The development of autonomous machine learning (ML) agents capable of end-to-end data science workflows represents a significant frontier in artificial intelligence. These agents must orchestrate complex sequences of data analysis, feature engineering, model selection, and hyperparameter optimization, tasks that require sophisticated planning and iteration. While recent work on building ML agents has explored using large language models (LLMs) for direct code generation, tool-augmented approaches offer greater modularity and reliability. However, existing tool-use benchmarks focus primarily on task-specific tool selection or argument extraction for tool invocation, failing to evaluate the sophisticated planning capabilities required for ML Agents. In this work, we introduce a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating tool-augmented ML agents using a curated set of 61 specialized tools and 15 tabular ML challenges from Kaggle. Our benchmark goes beyond traditional tool-use evaluation by incorporating an in-memory named object management, allowing agents to flexibly name, save, and retrieve intermediate results throughout the workflows. We demonstrate that standard ReAct-style approaches struggle to generate valid tool sequences for complex ML pipelines, and that tree search methods with LLM-based evaluation underperform due to inconsistent state scoring. To address these limitations, we propose two simple approaches: 1) using shaped deterministic rewards with structured textual feedback, and 2) decomposing the original problem into a sequence of sub-tasks, which significantly improves trajectory validity and task performance. Using GPT-4o, our approach improves over ReAct by 16.52 percentile positions, taking the median across all Kaggle challenges. We believe our work provides a foundation for developing more capable tool-augmented planning ML agents.

title: EM-Claw: An Experience-Grounded Language-Model Agent for Auto Cryo-EM Single-Particle Analysis
abstract: Single-particle cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) processing remains strongly dependent on expert judgement because difficult specimens often require dataset-specific strategies that cannot be captured by a fixed pipeline. Here we present EM-Claw, an experience-grounded multi-agent system for adaptive cryo-EM single-particle analysis. Rather than following a predefined workflow, EM-Claw retrieves processing precedents from previously solved datasets, consults external guidance, proposes and independently evaluates alternative strategies, executes CryoSPARC or RELION jobs, and revises the processing route according to quantitative and visual evidence. Human expertise can be introduced at any stage through natural-language instructions, while successful decisions and processing trajectories are retained as reusable experience. We evaluated EM-Claw on both publicly available cryo-EM datasets and experimental datasets collected in our laboratory, spanning soluble proteins, membrane proteins, GPCR complexes and small transporter monomers. Across these cases, EM-Claw adapted its processing strategies to specimen-specific challenges, including compositional heterogeneity, complex flexibility, preferred orientation and weak particle features. It produced reconstructions at higher resolution than previously published results (0.1~1.3 angstroms improvement) or solved structures that are now being prepared for publication, with no or little human intervention, thereby substantially reducing the time, effort and field experience required for human decision-making.

title: Merging Cyber Threat Intelligence Through Retrieval-Augmented Generation and Small Language Models for Rich Threat Representation
abstract: Cybersecurity operations rely on CTI from heterogeneous sources, such as structured threat representations and narrative reports. They describe adversarial behaviors but rarely make explicit the conditions that enable each attack step, the consequences it produces, and the evidence supporting them, leaving analysts to correlate fragmented information manually. Existing approaches extract entities, map tactics and techniques, or reconstruct attack chains; enriching attack steps with explicit, evidence-linked semantics remains largely unexplored. This paper presents a local-first pipeline for evidence-grounded attack-step enrichment that combines hybrid RAG with a locally deployed SLM. Starting from an analyst-provided attack representation and supporting CTI documents, the pipeline retrieves step-relevant evidence and generates enriched descriptions, pre-conditions, post-conditions, and traceable links to the supporting passages. The enriched steps are organized into graph that groups MITRE ATT&CK-aligned steps into tactic-level milestones. Explicit conditions help defenders block attacks by removing their enabling conditions and support detection by checking for their expected consequences. We evaluate the pipeline on ten public malware case studies derived from UK NCSC reports, using automated measurements and a structured manual assessment with annotations from two annotators. The results demonstrate that the pipeline is effective at generating conditions that are, for the most part, evidence-supported and meaningful w.r.t. the analyzed attack step. Similar considerations hold for the enriched descriptions. Finally, these findings demonstrate the feasibility of locally generating structured, evidence-grounded enrichments that improve the interpretability and traceability of attack step representations without requiring a manual reconstruction of attack execution.

title: Search From the Start: Search-Native Pretraining for Language Models
abstract: Modern language models (LMs) are increasingly deployed with access to search tools at inference. Yet pretraining remains predominantly focused on predicting static text, with search capabilities typically introduced during post-training. We propose Search-Native Pretraining as a practical route to teach search capability during pretraining from ordinary text corpora. Specifically, we augment pretraining corpus at scale with web-search queries and retrieve web response using a local index. Training on this augmented corpus teaches models to generate search calls and incorporate retrieved evidence during language modeling. Across Wikipedia and DCLM-Edu corpora and 360M to 3.3B parameter scales, search-pretrained models ("QueryLM") show improved performance on knowledge-intensive tasks and higher steerability toward the retrieved evidence. Crucially, their advantage persists after supervised fine-tuning of both search-pretrained and conventionally pretrained models, indicating that the tested post-training procedures do not fully recover the capabilities developed during pretraining. Throughout our experiments, we find that a 1.4B QueryLM consistently beats or matches the performance of a FLOP-matched 3.3B baseline model across all knowledge intensive tasks. These results establish search-pretraining as a practical way to develop foundational search capabilities during pretraining. We release the training artifacts, including model checkpoints and data.

title: Fine-tuned encoders, generative large language models and typed decisions for classifying findings in chest CT reports: paired English-Japanese internal testing and external testing on naturally written Japanese reports
abstract: PurposeTo compare fine-tuned encoders, generative large language models (LLMs) and typed decisions (per-finding yes/no questions answered with a probability) for classifying 18 findings in chest CT reports, and to identify when typed decisions help. MethodsThis retrospective study used public data. The internal test set comprised 150 CT-RATE reports with paired Japanese translations at three quality levels; the external test set, 243 naturally written Japanese reports with human annotations (RR-Findings). We compared ModernBERT encoders fine-tuned on 20,444 reports, generative LLMs (gpt-6-luna, Qwen3.8-27B, MedGemma), and typed decisions with Jev, the Decisions API and Qwen. Thresholds fixed on 450 development reports were applied unchanged externally. The primary metric was micro-F1; case-level paired bootstrap 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated for 11 internal comparisons. ResultsEncoders were best internally (English 0.9853; radiologist-checked Japanese 0.9576) and exceeded Jev (differences 0.0367, 95% CI 0.0258-0.0484; 0.0336, 0.0215-0.0464). Externally, Jev (0.8844) lay within the encoder seed range (0.8656-0.9144), exceeded the three generative conditions tested externally (best 0.8564) and the Decisions API (0.8177), and had the smallest internal-to-external decrease (-0.0396). An encoder trained on 2,044 reports reached 0.8226 externally. Typed-versus-generated differences changed direction across models and test sets. At a fixed threshold of 0.5, Jev fell to 0.7753 externally. ConclusionFine-tuned encoders performed best with ample in-distribution labels. Although threshold-dependent, Jev, with thresholds fitted on only 450 labeled reports, fell within the encoder seed range externally and exceeded the generative LLMs and an encoder trained on 2,044 reports, making it an option when labels are scarce.

title: Human-Centered Design and Evaluation of an LLM-based Decision Support Tool for Nurses in Rural India
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) perform well on physician reasoning tasks, sparking interest in using them to guide mid-level health providers where physicians are scarce. However, evidence is lacking for effective LLM interfaces and their performance in real patient encounters. We report the human-centered design and performance of the NurseAI mobile app in rural West Bengal, India. Nurses participated in six design rounds that culminated in an audio-based mobile app that listens to the patient interview in the patients native language, suggests patient-specific questions for the nurse, and generates an assessment and plan. Physician graders evaluated the apps output for fifty real-patient consultations in the final version and found 90% of the plans were appropriate, 96% valid, and 94% safe. Several feature improvements have been identified for future versions of the app from the field use.

title: From digital pathology to integrated precision oncology: AI-driven biomarker assessment and multimodal data integration in non-small cell lung cancer.
abstract: Digital pathology (DP) is evolving from an image-based diagnostic modality into a quantitative platform for computational precision oncology. This transition is particularly relevant in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), where limited tissue specimens must support histological classification, immunohistochemistry, broad molecular profiling and an expanding range of therapy-linked biomarkers. Artificial intelligence (AI) can assist conventional tasks such as tissue segmentation, cell detection, quality control and biomarker quantification, but it can also derive image-based signatures associated with molecular alterations, spatial immune organization and treatment response. This review focuses primarily on NSCLC and examines the continuum from foundational image-analysis tasks and AI-assisted PD-L1 scoring to histology-based molecular prediction, computational companion diagnostics, pathology foundation models and multimodal AI. We discuss recent lung-specific evidence, including computational triage of actionable alterations, the emerging TROP2 quantitative continuous scoring paradigm and selected protein biomarkers associated with antibody-drug conjugates. We also consider the integration of pathology with genomics, transcriptomics, liquid biopsy, radiology and longitudinal clinical data. Particular attention is given to the barriers separating algorithmic performance from clinical utility: uneven adoption of whole-slide imaging, pre-analytical and scanner variability, missing or asynchronous multimodal data, propagation of upstream measurement errors, laboratory information-system interoperability, prospective validation, regulation, reimbursement and equitable access. Emerging paradigms such as digital twins and agentic AI are discussed as research directions rather than established clinical tools. We argue that the principal value of AI in NSCLC will not be autonomous diagnosis, but the reliable conversion of fragmented data streams into transparent, auditable and clinically actionable patient representations.

title: Multifunctional Bioactivities of Ultrasound-Assisted Curcuma longa Oleoresin: Antioxidant, Antibacterial, Antibiofilm and Carrageenan-Induced Anti-Inflammatory Effects.
abstract: Ultrasound-assisted extraction (UAE), as a green and sustainable approach was used to enhance the phytochemical composition and biofunctional properties of Curcuma longa oleoresins. Curcuma rhizomes were subjected to UAE, using different organic solvents and the resulting oleoresins were evaluated for their phytochemical profile and multifunctional bioactivities. Among the tested solvents, ethanol produced the highest extraction yield (22.1%), followed by acetone and n-hexane. FTIR analysis revealed the presence of functional groups corresponding to phenolics, flavonoids and curcuminoids. GC-MS analysis tentatively characterized 31 bioactive compounds. Comparatively, ethanol extracted oleoresins demonstrated significantly higher total phenolic (4.66-8.87 GAE mg/g oleoresin) and flavonoid contents (7.74-12.19 CE µg/g oleoresin), supporting strong antioxidant potential, evaluated by 2,2-diphenyl-1-picrylhydrazyl, ferric reducing antioxidant power and hydrogen peroxide scavenging assays. All the oleoresins exhibited considerable antibacterial activity, with substantial biofilm inhibition (> 60%) at minimum inhibitory concentration values (0.312-1.25 µg/mL). Toxicological assessments indicated low hemolytic activity (< 5) and absence of mutagenicity at functional doses. Among the evaluated multimodal bioactivities, anti-inflammatory activity was most pronounced. In-vitro bovine serum albumin assay showed > 80% inhibition of protein denaturation. Furthermore, in-vivo carrageenan induced acute inflammation model in Wistar rats demonstrated significant dose-dependent anti-inflammatory effects through suppression of TNF-α (18.53 pg/mg protein), IL-6 (3.67 pg/mg protein) and restoration of antioxidant enzymes CAT (34.14 U/mg protein) and SOD (6.77 U/mg protein). Histopathological findings further demonstrated reduced inflammatory cell infiltration and tissue recovery. Overall, UAE effectively enhances the extraction yield and phytochemical richness profile of curcuma oleoresins, highlighting its potential as a safe natural anti-inflammatory agent for food and biomedical applications.

title: Challenges and opportunities in antimicrobial R&D.
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance is accelerating, while the discovery and development of new drugs, particularly those with novel mechanisms of action, have failed to keep pace. This widening gap reflects two major challenges: insufficient resources for antibiotic discovery and clinical development, and a lack of scientific innovation. With pharmaceutical companies largely abandoning antibiotic R&D, academic groups, small biotech companies, and not-for-profits are stepping in, harnessing advances in genomics, synthetic biology, and AI to drive discovery. Coupled with growing international investment and initiatives to address funding gaps, these efforts offer renewed hope for overcoming the antimicrobial resistance crisis.

title: HEmIF-Bench: Benchmarking H&E-to-mIF Models Beyond Virtual-Stain Fidelity
abstract: Hematoxylin and eosin (H&E)-to-multiplex immunofluorescence (mIF) generators predict spatial protein expression from routine histology, yet pixel-level marker reconstruction does not establish downstream utility. We present HEmIF-Bench, evaluating five frozen generators across eight datasets spanning molecular, cellular, tissue, and patient scales. HEmIF-Bench decouples internal encoder features from generated outputs, benchmarking both against the pathology foundation reference UNI2. Mirroring the clinical workflow where pathologists rely on mIF to define cell phenotypes, delineate tertiary lymphoid structures (TLSs) and germinal centers (GCs), and stratify patient risk, we evaluate external CD3 recovery, single-cell classification, dense nuclear segmentation, TLS/GC segmentation, and patient survival prediction. Across the benchmark, foundation-model-based MIPHEI-ViT leads among the generators, while non-foundation models show task-specific strengths. Comparing the two routes reveals that internal encoder features generally outperform generated outputs, and larger output marker panels do not guarantee stronger downstream utility across datasets. Moreover, neither internal encoder features nor generated outputs consistently surpass frozen UNI2. These findings show that pixel-level stain fidelity does not equate to downstream utility, and that generators trained at current paired-data scales have yet to surpass large-scale pure-H&E foundation models. With the expansion of paired translation cohorts and the advancement of foundation-based generative architectures, HEmIF-Bench establishes a definitive benchmark for tracking when H&E-to-mIF generation crosses the threshold to deliver genuine value beyond routine histology for tumor microenvironment analysis and precision oncology.

title: From Expanded Carrier Screening to Dynamic and Personalised Preconceptional Genomics.
abstract: Expanded carrier screening (ECS) has substantially broadened the scope of preconception genetic screening, but the expansion of fixed gene panels has also highlighted important limitations related to population diversity, genomic coverage, variant interpretation, residual risk and the clinical value of increasingly large panels. Recent advances in population genomics, sequencing technologies, longitudinal variant reassessment, quantitative risk assessment and artificial intelligence (AI) provide opportunities to move beyond static screening models. This review examines current challenges in ECS and explores the transition towards a more dynamic and individualised framework for preconceptional genomics. Rather than continually expanding fixed panels, genomic information could be selectively interpreted within the reproductive context and reassessed as knowledge, variant classifications and individual circumstances evolve. Emerging technologies, including exome- and long-read sequencing and AI-assisted variant interpretation, may facilitate this transition, although limitations related to validation, population diversity, penetrance and clinical interpretation remain. Genetic counselling and professional oversight will therefore remain essential to ensure that increasingly complex genomic information is translated into meaningful reproductive risk assessment and informed reproductive decision-making.

title: Volumetric Digital Microsphere Assay Coupling CbAgo-CRISPR/Cas12a and Lens-Free Holography for Salmonella typhimurium Detection.
abstract: Sensitive and precise quantification of foodborne pathogens in complex matrices remains challenging due to inefficient signal conversion, limited volumetric information, and inaccurate counting under dense signal conditions. Here, we develop an integrated digital biosensing platform that combines programmable biochemical amplification, lens-free holographic imaging, and intelligent computational decoding. A CbAgo-CRISPR/Cas12a cascade is employed to convert pathogen DNA signals into discrete microsphere-based digital outputs, while automated lens-free holography preserves three-dimensional spatial information for high-throughput acquisition. A depth-guided Transformer algorithm further enables accurate three-dimensional microsphere localization in dense sensing environments. Using Salmonella typhimurium as a model pathogen, the platform exhibited a linear response from 20 to 107 CFU/mL with a detection limit of 12 CFU/mL. The method showed good selectivity against the tested nontarget bacteria and was further evaluated in spiked chicken, egg, fish, and milk matrices, yielding quantitative results in good agreement with conventional plate counting. These results demonstrate a particle-based volumetric transduction strategy for digital biosensing in complex samples.

title: RIBOSPAN: A Long-Context RNA Foundation Model for Versatile RNA Modeling
abstract: Full-length RNAs, particularly messenger RNAs, often exceed the context lengths used to pretrain existing RNA foundation models, limiting complete-transcript modeling at single-nucleotide resolution. We present RIBOSPAN, a 1.61-billion-parameter bidirectional RNA foundation model natively pretrained with context lengths up to 10,240 nt, combining dense bidirectional self-attention with single-nucleotide tokenization. On a controlled long-context benchmark, native long-context pretraining maintains well-organized, context-specific representations across full transcripts, an advantage that inference-time extension of short-context models does not recover. RIBOSPAN learns state-of-the-art frozen RNA representations, and is the strongest encoder-only RNA foundation model in full-transcript property prediction and zero-shot mutation-fitness modeling. Without structural supervision during pretraining, its frozen backbone outperforms a fully fine-tuned structure-guided model on secondary structure prediction. Building on the same backbone, we develop a conditional discrete-diffusion framework for full-length mRNA generation and redesign. Together, RIBOSPAN establishes a powerful long-context foundation for transferable RNA representation learning, biological prediction, and full-transcript mRNA design.

title: MINE: A Training-Free Defense against Indirect Prompt Injection via Mutual Information and Embedding Variance
abstract: Existing defenses against indirect prompt injection in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) are inherently reactive: prompt-engineering methods are often overridden by the injected instructions, while supervised detectors must be retrained for each new attack style. We propose a different paradigm: defend by maximizing relevance, not by detecting attacks. Our method, MINE, is training-free and attack-agnostic, and it also serves as a query-conditioned reranker. To evaluate defenses under realistic conditions, we introduce LC-Inj-SQuAD, a long-context benchmark with an average of 4,032 words per context. We evaluate on four datasets spanning short-context QA (Inj-SQuAD, Inj-TriviaQA), long-context QA (LC-Inj-SQuAD), and agent tool-call injection (InjecAgent). Across all four, MINE achieves the best accuracy--security trade-off among training-free defenses. It is also the only defense that stays usable against a fully adaptive attacker, generalizes to agent tool-call injection, and achieves the lowest inference latency on long contexts.

title: GEM: A Generative Embedding Model Bridging Reasoning and Retrieval
abstract: Modern LLMs excel at reasoning and instruction following, enabling users to express increasingly complex information needs. However, existing retrievers largely rely on matching surface-level relevance, creating a growing gap between the evolving nature of user queries and how the queries are interpreted by retrievers. In this paper, we present GEM, a generative embedding model that augments retrieval by leveraging its internal knowledge to reason about user intent and relevance criteria prior to embedding. GEM unifies generation and embedding in a sequential manner, where encoding can be conceptually viewed as processing only one additional token during autoregressive generation. Unlike conventional query expansion, GEM learns to produce embeddings aligned with its reasoning, moving beyond surface-level matching. Furthermore, the generative nature allows GEM to be prompted like standard instruction-tuned LLMs and enables test-time compute scaling for retrieval. Compared with a non-reasoning variant of the same backbone, GEM achieves approximately 35% relative improvement in nDCG@10 on BRIGHT, a benchmark of challenging queries requiring reasoning, and 70% in p-MRR on FollowIR, a benchmark evaluating retrievers' ability to understand and follow user instructions. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of activating an embedding model's internal reasoning capabilities to improve retrieval. Our code and model are publicly available at https://github.com/ZhlSh17/GEM and https://huggingface.co/gem-search/GEM-4B, respectively.

title: DRAFT-ing Architectural Design Decisions using LLMs
abstract: Architectural Knowledge Management (AKM) is crucial for software development and Architectural Decision Records (ADR), an important artifact of AKM, provide a structured approach to capture Architectural Design Decisions (ADD). However, their adoption is limited due to the manual effort involved and insufficient tool support. Prior work shows that LLMs can support ADD generation, though basic prompting yields suboptimal results. This paper explores how LLMs can support architects in two complementary tasks: generating ADDs from Decision Contexts, and generating complete ADRs from titles. We propose Domain-specific Retrieval Augmented Few-shot Tuning (DRAFT), a novel approach that integrates Retrieval Augmented Few-shot Generation with Fine-tuning to generate. DRAFT operates in two phases: an offline phase that fine-tunes a model using retrieval-augmented prompts derived from historical ADRs, and an online phase that generates decisions or complete ADRs by combining retrieved examples with the fine-tuned model. Evaluated on 4344 ADRs across multiple LLMs using standard NLP metrics, DRAFT consistently produces outputs better aligned with real-world ADRs. A human evaluation with the authors and external architects, however, shows no uniformly preferred approach. DRAFT also maintains practical efficiency, reduces dependence- dence on proprietary models, and addresses organizational concerns around privacy, resource constraints, and inference costs.

title: CA-RAG: Constraint-Aligned Retrieval for Structurally Faithful Long-Form Generation
abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) typically optimises evidence selection for semantic relevance, whereas compliance-sensitive long-form generation also requires evidence supporting explicit structural obligations. Semantically relevant retrieval may therefore omit information needed for mandatory downstream clauses. We propose Constraint-Aligned RAG (CA-RAG), a retrieval-conditioning framework that augments section-specific queries with ontology-derived structural constraints and policy-grounded knowledge-graph relations before evidence selection. Retrieval-only evaluation with manually annotated evidence shows consistent improvements across retrieval budgets. At $k=6$, CA-RAG increases Precision@$k$ from $0.5268$ to $0.5692$, pooled Recall@$k$ from $0.5402$ to $0.5950$, and F1@$k$ from $0.5389$ to $0.5672$ over standard RAG. Generation experiments further show improvements in compliance and reliability in several model--domain settings, while generation-only constraints achieve higher clause coverage but lower overall compliance and reliability. These results indicate that structurally aligned retrieval can improve evidence sufficiency in compliance-sensitive long-form generation.
